newsitem.title: USA: Chastened Gingrich seeks to keep U.S. House power.
newsitem.headline: Chastened Gingrich seeks to keep U.S. House power.

text.p: Two years ago Newt Gingrich burst on the political firmament like an exploding star -- architect of a victory that produced the first Republican Congress in 40 years, rightwing visionary intent on remaking the U.S. government.

On Tuesday, as a new Congress convenes, he stands for re-election as speaker of the House of Representatives, chastened and badly weakened by political mistakes and by ethics violations that await the judgment of his colleagues.

Republican leaders predict Gingrich, 53, will retain his post with near-solid party backing. But the very next day, the Ethics Committee begins proceedings that will culminate later this month in an unprecedented House vote to punish a speaker.

Gingrich has agreed "with great sadness" with an ethics subcommittee's finding that tax-exempt funds helped to finance a partisan lecture series he conducted -- legally, the charge is that he failed to prevent this -- and that he then gave investigators misleading information on that matter.
But the ethics flap is only the latest of his problems.
His uncharacteristically contrite admission followed a November election in which Democrats tried to demonise him as the man who wanted to cut Medicare old-age health insurance.
Some Republicans shunned him in their own campaigns.

The Medicare attacks, two partial shutdowns of the U.S. government in a budget dispite with President Bill Clinton last winter -- for which voters mostly blamed the Republicans -- and failed efforts to roll back environmental laws helped reduce the party's House majority in the election.
Thomas Mann, a Congress expert at Washington's Brookings Institution, said Gingrich's role had diminished even before the ethics controversy and predicted the trend would continue.
"There's no repeating the extraordinary start to his speakership in early 1995," Mann said in an interview. "He had an extraordiary run but it was a very short one."
For Gingrich that translates into a conciliatory stance.

"We have an absolute moral obligation to make this system work," he told Republicans who re-nominated him for the speaker's post in November. "I want to suggest to you that if the last Congress was the confrontation Congress, this Congress will be the implementation Congress."

It was quite a change of tone for the Georgia congressman and former university professor, who made his name as a House "bomb-thrower" and ethics warrior and forced the resignation of Democratic Speaker Jim Wright on ethics charges in 1989.
Gingrich took the speaker's gavel himself two years ago to his supporters' chants of "Newt! Newt! Newt!" after a 1994 election that ended a 40-year Democratic monopoly on the post.

His round face, rapid-fire speech and thatch of gray hair became a regular feature of the political scene. He led a profound change in the terms of the political debate in which cutting spending and balancing the budget became paramount.

Under his leadership the Republican revolution swung into a frenetic first 100 days in which the House voted on its Contract with America, a list of 10 legislative initiatives. Some key items never became law, but Gingrich made a habit of triumphantly pulling a laminated card from his pocket and marking the Contract's progress.
The high-profile speaker was even the subject of speculation as a possible 1996 presidential candidate and was Time magazine's "man of the year" cover story subject for 1995.

But with fame came controversy. First came his acceptance of a $4.5 million advance for his book, "To Renew America." He bowed to widespread criticism and turned down the advance, but the Ethics Committee chided him for "what some could describe an attempt by you to capitalise on your office."
Then Gingrich was mocked by a newspaper as a crybaby for complaining that, on a trip aboard Air Force One, Clinton had not invited him to join him in the front of the plane.

Democrats, meanwhile, did not forgive Gingrich for denouncing Congress as "corrupt" under their rule and for his role in the downfall of Wright. Democratic Whip David Bonior filed a blizzard of ethics complaints against him.
Most were dismissed, some led to letters of mild rebuke.

If he is re-elected as expected on Tuesday he will be the first Republican to be elected speaker in successive Congresses since the 1920s. About two weeks later he will become the first speaker to face punishment by the House.
